The newly hatched Red-chested cuckoo chick emerges from an egg incubated at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] after an incubation period of approximately 11.5 days [ab = approximately 11.5 days], a developmental duration somewhat shorter than that reported for its congener Cuculus canorus. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling possesses a remarkably low initial wet weight of just 3.22 grams [Ww0 = 3.22 grams], reflecting the relatively small egg size characteristic of many brood-parasitic Cuculidae. This modest neonatal mass necessitates a rapid phase of mass gain driven by the intensive provisioning efforts of the unwitting host parents, which must supply sufficient insect prey to support the demanding growth trajectory of the parasitic chick. The chick's development during the first days of exotrophic life is marked by a swift increase in body size, as the nestling transitions from a state of complete dependency to one capable of sustained begging and competitive displacement of host offspring. The energetic efficiency of this early growth phase is likely linked to the stable thermal microclimate provided by the host's nest, which buffers environmental fluctuations and allows the chick to allocate ingested resources primarily toward somatic tissue synthesis rather than thermoregulatory costs during these critical early stages.

Almost immediately upon achieving nutritional independence from the host parents, the juvenile cuckoo begins a phase of rapid somatic development that culminates in the fledging stage. In the Red-chested cuckoo, this milestone is reached at just 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching] under the elevated body temperatures typical of an actively metabolizing nestling, approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which facilitates efficient muscle and feather development. This remarkably brief nestling period, among the shortest recorded for any cuckoo species of comparable adult size, allows the young bird to vacate the host nest before potential detection by the host parents or predators. Following fledging, the young cuckoo enters a period of extended dependency during which it continues to solicit food from its hosts while gradually refining its foraging skills and flight capabilities. The transition to complete independence is a gradual process, with post-fledging parental care often persisting for several weeks as the juvenile bird hones its ability to locate and capture insect prey on its own. This prolonged post-fledging association with hosts, unusual among most passerine species, appears to be a key adaptation that compensates for the absence of species-specific parental guidance in the parasitic cuckoo's life history.

Sexual maturation in the Red-chested cuckoo proceeds along a distinct developmental timeline, with puberty attained at approximately 57 days after hatching [tp = approximately 57 days after hatching] when maintained at a typical active metabolic temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. At this stage, the gonads undergo rapid development, and the young bird begins to exhibit the characteristic vocalizations and territorial behaviors associated with breeding readiness. However, despite the relatively early onset of physiological reproductive capability, first breeding is typically deferred to a much later age. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at the same thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], indicating that while puberty is reached within weeks of fledging, actual reproductive effort is generally postponed until the following breeding season. This delay is likely adaptive, providing the young cuckoo with an extended period for gaining familiarity with local host populations, establishing a home range, and accumulating sufficient body reserves to support the energetically demanding process of egg production and brood parasitism. The discrepancy between the ages at physiological maturity and first reproduction underscores the complex interplay between intrinsic developmental programs and extrinsic ecological constraints shaping the species' reproductive strategy.

Adult body mass in the Red-chested cuckoo exhibits modest sexual dimorphism, with males typically attaining a slightly larger ultimate size compared to females. Field surveys and museum specimen data indicate that the ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 75.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 75.3 grams], whereas females generally achieve a slightly lower asymptotic mass of around 71.6 grams [Wwi = around 71.6 grams]. This difference in adult body mass, though relatively small in absolute terms, may reflect divergent selective pressures operating on the two sexes; for males, larger body size may confer advantages in territory defense and mate attraction, while females may benefit from a more streamlined body plan that enhances maneuverability during the rapid, targeted egg-laying visits to host nests. The species' overall adult mass range places it among the medium-sized members of the genus Cuculus, broadly comparable to the better-studied common cuckoo Cuculus canorus. The attainment of this ultimate mass occurs gradually over the first year of life, with fledglings already exhibiting substantial growth before reaching their definitive adult dimensions, which are maintained throughout most of the reproductive lifespan.

This maximum lifespan of nearly 13 years is comparable to that of other medium-sized parasitic cuckoos, although exact records for Cuculus solitarius remain sparse due to the challenges of long-term monitoring of brood-parasitic species that do not maintain permanent territories. Throughout this extended adult phase, the reproductive output of females is constrained by the availability of suitable host nests and the energetic demands of egg production.
